Well, it's... I mean, if I really stop and analyze it, which I do, probably way too much honestly, it's this overwhelming feeling that I'm going to get stuck in there. Or worse, that the cables are just going to snap and the whole thing is going to free-fall. 

I know, I know exactly how it sounds. Like, logically, I'm a pretty rational guy, right? I teach people how to use complex software, I deal with logic and step-by-step processes all day long. So, intellectually, I know that an elevator in a big modern office block is probably perfectly safe. They have emergency brakes and backup systems and strict maintenance schedules and all that stuff. I've actually read up on elevator engineering online, just trying to convince myself that it's fine and that the math is on my side. 

But then... then I look at the elevators in my apartment building, or even the ones in some of the older buildings where I'm supposed to do these training workshops, and they have those heavy, old metal doors that kind of shudder and scrape when they close. And the moment I see those old doors, all that logic just completely flies out the window. My brain just short-circuits. It's like my mind treats it as an absolute certainty that if I step inside, those doors are going to jam shut, and I'll be trapped in this tiny, suffocating metal box for hours, or the floor is just going to drop out from under me into the shaft. 

And it's incredibly frustrating because there's this rational part of me standing there in the lobby saying, "Hey, this sounds completely over the top, people ride these things thousands of times a day without a second thought." But the rest of my brain is just screaming that it's a trap. I just stand there staring at the little gap between the hallway floor and the elevator car, thinking about the mechanics failing, and I just can't make my legs step across it. I just can't do it.

Yeah, actually... yeah, there was. It's kind of the whole reason this started, honestly. It was about seven months ago, right around the time I moved into this new apartment. The one on the fifth floor. 

Moving day was a total nightmare to begin with. It was the middle of summer, super hot, and I had rented this U-Haul truck and managed to rope a couple of buddies into helping me. We had been hauling boxes and furniture all day, sweating buckets, just completely exhausted. And we were finally on the last trip. We had loaded my couch onto this dolly—it's this really heavy, awkward sectional piece, you know the kind that never quite fits through doorways right? Anyway, we get it into the elevator on the ground floor. It was a tight squeeze, but we managed it. 

So it's me, my two friends, and this massive couch crammed into this tiny elevator car. I press the button for the fifth floor, the doors close with that awful scraping sound I mentioned earlier, and we start going up. We get to about the third floor, and suddenly, the whole car just jerks. Like, a violent, hard stop that almost knocked us off our feet. The lights flickered, and then everything just went dead. The hum of the motor, the little floor indicator light, everything. Just total silence and darkness, except for the emergency light which was this weird, sickly yellow color and barely illuminated anything.

At first, we thought it was a joke or just a quick power blip, you know? We were kind of laughing it off, making jokes about being trapped. But then five minutes went by. Then ten. It was incredibly hot in there with three guys and a giant couch, and the air just felt instantly stale. I tried pressing the emergency call button, but nothing happened. It was completely dead. We started banging on the doors, yelling for help, but the walls in that building are so thick, it felt like nobody could hear us. 

I just remember looking at the doors, realizing there was literally no way to pry them open from the inside without power, and feeling this cold sweat break out all over me. My heart started pounding so hard I could feel it in my ears. I kept thinking about the cables, wondering if that violent jerk meant something had snapped. I was convinced the car was going to plummet at any second. My friends were trying to stay calm, but I was just totally losing it. I felt like I couldn't breathe. 

We were stuck in there for two hours. Two whole hours before the fire department finally managed to manually pry the doors open from the fourth-floor hallway and pull us out. I was shaking so badly I could barely stand. Ever since that day—so, yeah, for the last seven months—I just haven't been able to set foot in an elevator. The mere thought of it brings back that feeling of being trapped in that yellow light, waiting to fall.

They are super cramped, barely enough room to turn around, and the servers are just humming and blowing hot air everywhere, so it's loud and really stuffy. But I can sit in there on the floor for an hour untangling wires and it doesn't even cross my mind to be anxious. Because the door is right there, you know? It's the suspension, the mechanics of being hoisted up in the air by wires in a box that you can't manually open from the inside if the power cuts out. The one on the fifth floor. \n\nMoving day was a total nightmare to begin with. We had loaded my couch onto this dolly—it's this really heavy, awkward sectional piece, you know the kind that never quite fits through doorways right? Anyway, we get it into the elevator on the ground floor. It was a tight squeeze, but we managed it. \n\nSo it's me, my two friends, and this massive couch crammed into this tiny elevator car. I press the button for the fifth floor, the doors close with that awful scraping sound I mentioned earlier, and we start going up. The hum of the motor, the little floor indicator light, everything. Just total silence and darkness, except for the emergency light which was this weird, sickly yellow color and barely illuminated anything.\n\nAt first, we thought it was a joke or just a quick power blip, you know? ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
No, heights don't bother me at all. It's funny, right? You'd think, given the whole elevator thing and the fear of falling, that being up high would be a huge trigger. But it's really not. Like, a couple of weeks ago, I was actually at this rooftop bar downtown for a buddy's birthday—the same buddy who was stuck in the elevator with me, actually, which is kind of ironic. But anyway, this place was on the twentieth floor of this huge high-rise. I took the stairs all the way up, which, let me tell you, was a serious workout, I was completely drenched in sweat by the time I got there. 

But once I was up there? Totally fine. I walked right up to the edge of the patio. They had this glass railing, you know, the kind that's completely transparent so you can see straight down to the street below. Cars looking like little ants, people walking around, the whole city spread out. And I stood right against that glass, looking straight down, and I didn't feel a single flutter in my stomach. No racing heart, no sweaty palms, nothing. I actually thought it was a pretty incredible view. I even leaned over a little bit to point out a landmark to my friend. 

And it's the same thing with high windows. In my apartment, I'm on the fifth floor, which isn't crazy high, but it's high enough. Sometimes I just stand by the window in my living room, drinking my coffee in the morning, looking out over the parking lot and the trees, and it's actually really peaceful. I've even been up in the Willis Tower in Chicago—well, a few years ago, before the elevator thing started, obviously, because there's no way I'd take an elevator up 100 floors now. But when I was up there, standing in those glass boxes that stick out from the side of the building? I thought it was awesome. 

So yeah, it's definitely not the height itself. I think it all comes back to the control aspect, or the mechanics of it. When I'm standing on a roof or looking out a window, I know the building is solid. It's built into the ground, it's not going anywhere. I'm standing on concrete or steel that is fundamentally stationary. But an elevator is just a box dangling on a string, you know? It's the suspension, the fact that the only thing keeping me from plummeting is a set of cables and pulleys that I can't see and have no control over. The height is just the consequence of the fall, not the thing that actually scares me. If that makes any sense.

Honestly, no. Not at all. I mean, when you feel like you're about to drop five stories down a dark shaft, you really couldn't care less if the guy next to you thinks you're acting weird, you know? It's like total survival mode just completely takes over your brain.

My brain is just screaming, "Danger, get out, the cables are snapping." It's entirely about the mechanical failure and the falling. That’s a really interesting question, actually, because you’d think so, right? Like, logically, if I have a big red button that says "manual override" or a phone that I know for an absolute fact goes straight to a 911 dispatcher or a building manager, that should make me feel better. It’s so frustrating because it’s like my brain has just completely short-circuited when it comes to this one specific thing. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Man, a freight elevator... you know, we actually have one of those at the corporate office I was telling you about. It's this big, industrial thing they use for moving heavy desks and all our training equipment, and it's got those heavy wooden gates you have to pull down yourself, and a lever. So, you'd think, okay, I'm the one pulling the gate, I'm the one holding the lever, I'm basically driving the thing, right? That should fix it. 

But honestly? No. I really don't think it would make a lick of difference. And the reason is... it's just how fast the fear hits me. It's not this logical process where I stand there and evaluate who has control of the machinery. 

It's like... as soon as I even step toward an elevator, literally any elevator, or—God, especially if I just hear that heavy metal *clunk* when the doors start to open—it's just game over. My chest just completely tightens up. It feels like someone strapped a belt around my ribs and pulled it tight. And my hands get instantly sweaty, just completely clammy, which is gross, I know, but it happens every single time. I just feel this absolute, overwhelming rush of panic, and it happens before I’ve even had a split second to think it through. 

So, before my brain can even say, "Hey, it's cool, you're operating this freight elevator, you have the lever," my body is already in full meltdown mode. It's like my nervous system doesn't care who's in charge. It just hears that *clunk* and goes, "Nope, we're in danger." I remember one time I was just walking past the freight elevator at work, not even intending to use it, just carrying some training binders to the stairwell, and one of the maintenance guys called it. Just hearing the gears grind and the doors clatter open... bam. Sweaty hands, tight chest, that huge rush of panic. I had to just stand there for a second. 

So yeah, manual control sounds great in theory, but when the panic hits you that fast, before you even cross the threshold, having a lever to pull just doesn't matter at all. Because by the time I'd even get my hands on that lever, I'm already terrified.

I'm in control of the vehicle, or at least, I know gravity isn't going to suddenly pull me down a fifty-foot empty shaft. \n\nAnd small rooms are totally fine, too. At my job, doing the computer training stuff, sometimes I have to go into these tiny little server closets to check on equipment or trace a network issue. They are super cramped, barely enough room to turn around, and the servers are just humming and blowing hot air everywhere, so it's loud and really stuffy. But I can sit in there on the floor for an hour untangling wires and it doesn't even cross my mind to be anxious. Because the door is right there, you know? It's on a normal hinge, I can just turn the handle and walk out onto a solid, stationary floor. \n\nIt really is just the elevators. It's the suspension, the mechanics of being hoisted up in the air by wires in a box that you can't manually open from the inside if the power cuts out. So yeah, enclosed spaces generally aren't the issue at all. It's just that one very specific situation.\n\nDoctor: Has anything bad or frightening ever happened to you involving an elevator?\n\nPatient: Yeah, actually... yeah, there was. It's kind of the whole reason this started, honestly. It was about seven months ago, right around the time I moved into this new apartment. The one on the fifth floor. \n\nMoving day was a total nightmare to begin with. It was the middle of summer, super hot, and I had rented this U-Haul truck and managed to rope a couple of buddies into helping me. We had been hauling boxes and furniture all day, sweating buckets, just completely exhausted. And we were finally on the last trip. We had loaded my couch onto this dolly—it's this really heavy, awkward sectional piece, you know the kind that never quite fits through doorways right? Anyway, we get it into the elevator on the ground floor. It was a tight squeeze, but we managed it. \n\nSo it's me, my two friends, and this massive couch crammed into this tiny elevator car. I press the button for the fifth floor, the doors close with that awful scraping sound I mentioned earlier, and we start going up. We get to about the third floor, and suddenly, the whole car just jerks. Like, a violent, hard stop that almost knocked us off our feet. The lights flickered, and then everything just went dead. The hum of the motor, the little floor indicator light, everything. Just total silence and darkness, except for the emergency light which was this weird, sickly yellow color and barely illuminated anything.\n\nAt first, we thought it was a joke or just a quick power blip, you know? We were kind of laughing it off, making jokes about being trapped. But then five minutes went by. Then ten. It was incredibly hot in there with three guys and a giant couch, and the air just felt instantly stale. I tried pressing the emergency call button, but nothing happened. It was completely dead. We started banging on the doors, yelling for help, but the walls in that building are so thick, it felt like nobody could hear us. \n\nI just remember looking at the doors, realizing there was literally no way to pry them open from the inside without power, and feeling this cold sweat break out all over me. My heart started pounding so hard I could feel it in my ears. I kept thinking about the cables, wondering if that violent jerk meant something had snapped. I was convinced the car was going to plummet at any second. My friends were trying to stay calm, but I was just totally losing it. I felt like I couldn't breathe. \n\nWe were stuck in there for two hours. Two whole hours before the fire department finally managed to manually pry the doors open from the fourth-floor hallway and pull us out. I was shaking so badly I could barely stand. Ever since that day—so, yeah, for the last seven months—I just haven't been able to set foot in an elevator. The mere thought of it brings back that feeling of being trapped in that yellow light, waiting to fall.\n\nDoctor: When you're in a situation where you have to be in a high place, like standing near a ledge or looking out a high window, do you feel anxious or fearful?\n\nPatient: No, heights don't bother me at all. It's funny, right? You'd think, given the whole elevator thing and the fear of falling, that being up high would be a huge trigger. But it's really not. Like, a couple of weeks ago, I was actually at this rooftop bar downtown for a buddy's birthday—the same buddy who was stuck in the elevator with me, actually, which is kind of ironic. But anyway, this place was on the twentieth floor of this huge high-rise. I took the stairs all the way up, which, let me tell you, was a serious workout, I was completely drenched in sweat by the time I got there. \n\nBut once I was up there? Totally fine. I walked right up to the edge of the patio. They had this glass railing, you know, the kind that's completely transparent so you can see straight down to the street below. Cars looking like little ants, people walking around, the whole city spread out. And I stood right against that glass, looking straight down, and I didn't feel a single flutter in my stomach. No racing heart, no sweaty palms, nothing. I actually thought it was a pretty incredible view. I even leaned over a little bit to point out a landmark to my friend. \n\nAnd it's the same thing with high windows. In my apartment, I'm on the fifth floor, which isn't crazy high, but it's high enough. Sometimes I just stand by the window in my living room, drinking my coffee in the morning, looking out over the parking lot and the trees, and it's actually really peaceful. I've even been up in the Willis Tower in Chicago—well, a few years ago, before the elevator thing started, obviously, because there's no way I'd take an elevator up 100 floors now. But when I was up there, standing in those glass boxes that stick out from the side of the building? I thought it was awesome. \n\nSo yeah, it's definitely not the height itself. I think it all comes back to the control aspect, or the mechanics of it. When I'm standing on a roof or looking out a window, I know the building is solid. It's built into the ground, it's not going anywhere. I'm standing on concrete or steel that is fundamentally stationary. But an elevator is just a box dangling on a string, you know? It's the suspension, the fact that the only thing keeping me from plummeting is a set of cables and pulleys that I can't see and have no control over. The height is just the consequence of the fall, not the thing that actually scares me. If that makes any sense.\n\nDoctor: Do you worry about what other people might think of you if you were to have a panic attack or exhibit anxious behavior while in an elevator?\n\nPatient: Honestly, no. Not at all. I mean, when you feel like you're about to drop five stories down a dark shaft, you really couldn't care less if the guy next to you thinks you're acting weird, you know? It's like total survival mode just completely takes over your brain. \n\nI remember when I was stuck in there with my friends—like I was telling you before, the two guys who were helping me move—I was completely losing it. I was sweating, breathing heavy, practically pacing in this tiny little space next to that giant couch, and I didn't give a single, solitary thought to whether they thought I was being uncool or weak or whatever. And these are guys I usually joke around with all the time, guys where you normally wouldn't want to look like a wimp in front of them, right? There's usually a lot of, you know, typical guy banter, giving each other a hard time. But in that moment? Nothing. I just wanted out. If I had to scream and cry to get those doors open, I would have done it without a second thought. \n\nSo, no, the social aspect of it, like being embarrassed or worrying about strangers judging me if I were to freak out... it doesn't even register on my radar. My brain is just screaming, \"Danger, get out, the cables are snapping.\" It's entirely about the mechanical failure and the falling. If I were to ever get in one again—which, let's be real, I'm absolutely not planning on doing anytime soon—and I started hyperventilating or panicking, the absolute last thing on my mind would be whether someone in a suit next to me thinks I look crazy. I'd just be entirely focused on not dying in a metal box. The fear is 100 percent about the elevator itself, not the people in it.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your fear would decrease if you were in an elevator with a manual override or an emergency phone that you could use in case something went wrong?\n\nPatient: That’s a really interesting question, actually, because you’d think so, right? Like, logically, if I have a big red button that says \"manual override\" or a phone that I know for an absolute fact goes straight to a 911 dispatcher or a building manager, that should make me feel better. Because, like I was saying earlier, when we were stuck, the emergency button in that car was totally dead. Just nothing happened when I pushed it. So having a working one *should* be the magic fix. \n\nBut... honestly? I really don't think it would matter. It’s so frustrating because it’s like my brain has just completely short-circuited when it comes to this one specific thing. I mean, I know, logically speaking, that an elevator in a big, modern office block is probably completely safe. They have all the updated tech, the magnetic safety brakes, the working emergency phones, the regular inspections, all of that stuff. I get that. But it doesn't seem to make a difference to my gut reaction. \n\nLike, when I look at those heavy, old, scraping doors in my apartment building, or even the ones at my work—I'm a training and development specialist, and our corporate office is in this older building downtown that really hasn't been properly renovated since maybe the late nineties—my mind just instantly goes into full-blown panic mode. It just completely treats the situation like I’m about to get trapped in there for hours in the dark again, or worse, that the cables are going to snap and I'm going to be dropped straight down the shaft. \n\nAnd the craziest part of the whole thing is, part of me *knows* that sounds completely over the top. I’m a rational guy, you know? I’ll be standing there in the lobby, looking at the doors, and my rational brain is sitting there saying, \"Come on, man, thousands of people ride these every single day, the odds of it falling are basically zero.\" But my body and my subconscious are just screaming that it's a death trap. It's this weird split in my head. The logic of a safety feature just doesn't even touch the fear, if that makes sense.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your fear of elevators would be lessened if you were the one operating the elevator, such as in a freight elevator where you have manual control?\n\nPatient: Man, a freight elevator... you know, we actually have one of those at the corporate office I was telling you about. It's this big, industrial thing they use for moving heavy desks and all our training equipment, and it's got those heavy wooden gates you have to pull down yourself, and a lever. So, you'd think, okay, I'm the one pulling the gate, I'm the one holding the lever, I'm basically driving the thing, right? That should fix it. \n\nBut honestly? No. I really don't think it would make a lick of difference. And the reason is... it's just how fast the fear hits me. It's not this logical process where I stand there and evaluate who has control of the machinery. \n\nIt's like... as soon as I even step toward an elevator, literally any elevator, or—God, especially if I just hear that heavy metal *clunk* when the doors start to open—it's just game over. No, honestly, not at all. Which is... I mean, it’s kind of funny when you think about it, because you'd assume that if I freak out that badly over an elevator, I'd be a nervous wreck about everything else where I'm not in the driver's seat, right? But I'm really not.

But I can sit in there on the floor for an hour untangling wires and it doesn't even cross my mind to be anxious. Because the door is right there, you know? It's on a normal hinge, I can just turn the handle and walk out onto a solid, stationary floor. \n\nIt really is just the elevators. It's the suspension, the mechanics of being hoisted up in the air by wires in a box that you can't manually open from the inside if the power cuts out. So yeah, enclosed spaces generally aren't the issue at all. It's just that one very specific situation.\n\nDoctor: Has anything bad or frightening ever happened to you involving an elevator?\n\nPatient: Yeah, actually... yeah, there was. It's kind of the whole reason this started, honestly. It was about seven months ago, right around the time I moved into this new apartment. The one on the fifth floor. \n\nMoving day was a total nightmare to begin with. It was the middle of summer, super hot, and I had rented this U-Haul truck and managed to rope a couple of buddies into helping me. We had been hauling boxes and furniture all day, sweating buckets, just completely exhausted. And we were finally on the last trip. We had loaded my couch onto this dolly—it's this really heavy, awkward sectional piece, you know the kind that never quite fits through doorways right? Anyway, we get it into the elevator on the ground floor. It was a tight squeeze, but we managed it. \n\nSo it's me, my two friends, and this massive couch crammed into this tiny elevator car. I press the button for the fifth floor, the doors close with that awful scraping sound I mentioned earlier, and we start going up. We get to about the third floor, and suddenly, the whole car just jerks. Like, a violent, hard stop that almost knocked us off our feet. The lights flickered, and then everything just went dead. The hum of the motor, the little floor indicator light, everything. Just total silence and darkness, except for the emergency light which was this weird, sickly yellow color and barely illuminated anything.\n\nAt first, we thought it was a joke or just a quick power blip, you know? We were kind of laughing it off, making jokes about being trapped. But then five minutes went by. Then ten. It was incredibly hot in there with three guys and a giant couch, and the air just felt instantly stale. I tried pressing the emergency call button, but nothing happened. It was completely dead. We started banging on the doors, yelling for help, but the walls in that building are so thick, it felt like nobody could hear us. \n\nI just remember looking at the doors, realizing there was literally no way to pry them open from the inside without power, and feeling this cold sweat break out all over me. My heart started pounding so hard I could feel it in my ears. I kept thinking about the cables, wondering if that violent jerk meant something had snapped. I was convinced the car was going to plummet at any second. My friends were trying to stay calm, but I was just totally losing it. I felt like I couldn't breathe. \n\nWe were stuck in there for two hours. Two whole hours before the fire department finally managed to manually pry the doors open from the fourth-floor hallway and pull us out. I was shaking so badly I could barely stand. Ever since that day—so, yeah, for the last seven months—I just haven't been able to set foot in an elevator. The mere thought of it brings back that feeling of being trapped in that yellow light, waiting to fall.\n\nDoctor: When you're in a situation where you have to be in a high place, like standing near a ledge or looking out a high window, do you feel anxious or fearful?\n\nPatient: No, heights don't bother me at all. It's funny, right? You'd think, given the whole elevator thing and the fear of falling, that being up high would be a huge trigger. But it's really not. Like, a couple of weeks ago, I was actually at this rooftop bar downtown for a buddy's birthday—the same buddy who was stuck in the elevator with me, actually, which is kind of ironic. But anyway, this place was on the twentieth floor of this huge high-rise. I took the stairs all the way up, which, let me tell you, was a serious workout, I was completely drenched in sweat by the time I got there. \n\nBut once I was up there? Totally fine. I walked right up to the edge of the patio. They had this glass railing, you know, the kind that's completely transparent so you can see straight down to the street below. Cars looking like little ants, people walking around, the whole city spread out. And I stood right against that glass, looking straight down, and I didn't feel a single flutter in my stomach. No racing heart, no sweaty palms, nothing. I actually thought it was a pretty incredible view. I even leaned over a little bit to point out a landmark to my friend. \n\nAnd it's the same thing with high windows. In my apartment, I'm on the fifth floor, which isn't crazy high, but it's high enough. Sometimes I just stand by the window in my living room, drinking my coffee in the morning, looking out over the parking lot and the trees, and it's actually really peaceful. I've even been up in the Willis Tower in Chicago—well, a few years ago, before the elevator thing started, obviously, because there's no way I'd take an elevator up 100 floors now. But when I was up there, standing in those glass boxes that stick out from the side of the building? I thought it was awesome. \n\nSo yeah, it's definitely not the height itself. I think it all comes back to the control aspect, or the mechanics of it. When I'm standing on a roof or looking out a window, I know the building is solid. It's built into the ground, it's not going anywhere. I'm standing on concrete or steel that is fundamentally stationary. But an elevator is just a box dangling on a string, you know? It's the suspension, the fact that the only thing keeping me from plummeting is a set of cables and pulleys that I can't see and have no control over. The height is just the consequence of the fall, not the thing that actually scares me. If that makes any sense.\n\nDoctor: Do you worry about what other people might think of you if you were to have a panic attack or exhibit anxious behavior while in an elevator?\n\nPatient: Honestly, no. Not at all. I mean, when you feel like you're about to drop five stories down a dark shaft, you really couldn't care less if the guy next to you thinks you're acting weird, you know? It's like total survival mode just completely takes over your brain. \n\nI remember when I was stuck in there with my friends—like I was telling you before, the two guys who were helping me move—I was completely losing it. I was sweating, breathing heavy, practically pacing in this tiny little space next to that giant couch, and I didn't give a single, solitary thought to whether they thought I was being uncool or weak or whatever. And these are guys I usually joke around with all the time, guys where you normally wouldn't want to look like a wimp in front of them, right? There's usually a lot of, you know, typical guy banter, giving each other a hard time. But in that moment? Nothing. I just wanted out. If I had to scream and cry to get those doors open, I would have done it without a second thought. \n\nSo, no, the social aspect of it, like being embarrassed or worrying about strangers judging me if I were to freak out... it doesn't even register on my radar. My brain is just screaming, \"Danger, get out, the cables are snapping.\" It's entirely about the mechanical failure and the falling. If I were to ever get in one again—which, let's be real, I'm absolutely not planning on doing anytime soon—and I started hyperventilating or panicking, the absolute last thing on my mind would be whether someone in a suit next to me thinks I look crazy. I'd just be entirely focused on not dying in a metal box. The fear is 100 percent about the elevator itself, not the people in it.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your fear would decrease if you were in an elevator with a manual override or an emergency phone that you could use in case something went wrong?\n\nPatient: That’s a really interesting question, actually, because you’d think so, right? Because, like I was saying earlier, when we were stuck, the emergency button in that car was totally dead. Just nothing happened when I pushed it. So having a working one *should* be the magic fix. \n\nBut... honestly? I really don't think it would matter. It’s so frustrating because it’s like my brain has just completely short-circuited when it comes to this one specific thing. They have all the updated tech, the magnetic safety brakes, the working emergency phones, the regular inspections, all of that stuff. I get that. But it doesn't seem to make a difference to my gut reaction. \n\nLike, when I look at those heavy, old, scraping doors in my apartment building, or even the ones at my work—I'm a training and development specialist, and our corporate office is in this older building downtown that really hasn't been properly renovated since maybe the late nineties—my mind just instantly goes into full-blown panic mode. It just completely treats the situation like I’m about to get trapped in there for hours in the dark again, or worse, that the cables are going to snap and I'm going to be dropped straight down the shaft. \n\nAnd the craziest part of the whole thing is, part of me *knows* that sounds completely over the top. I’m a rational guy, you know? I’ll be standing there in the lobby, looking at the doors, and my rational brain is sitting there saying, \"Come on, man, thousands of people ride these every single day, the odds of it falling are basically zero.\" But my body and my subconscious are just screaming that it's a death trap. It's this weird split in my head. So even if you put a giant, state-of-the-art emergency phone right in the middle of the wall, or gave me a manual steering wheel for the thing, I’d still be looking at those old doors feeling like I was about to plummet. The logic of a safety feature just doesn't even touch the fear, if that makes sense.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your fear of elevators would be lessened if you were the one operating the elevator, such as in a freight elevator where you have manual control?\n\nPatient: Man, a freight elevator... you know, we actually have one of those at the corporate office I was telling you about. It's this big, industrial thing they use for moving heavy desks and all our training equipment, and it's got those heavy wooden gates you have to pull down yourself, and a lever. So, you'd think, okay, I'm the one pulling the gate, I'm the one holding the lever, I'm basically driving the thing, right? That should fix it. \n\nBut honestly? No. I really don't think it would make a lick of difference. And the reason is... it's just how fast the fear hits me. It's not this logical process where I stand there and evaluate who has control of the machinery. \n\nIt's like... as soon as I even step toward an elevator, literally any elevator, or—God, especially if I just hear that heavy metal *clunk* when the doors start to open—it's just game over. My chest just completely tightens up. It feels like someone strapped a belt around my ribs and pulled it tight. And my hands get instantly sweaty, just completely clammy, which is gross, I know, but it happens every single time. I just feel this absolute, overwhelming rush of panic, and it happens before I’ve even had a split second to think it through. \n\nSo, before my brain can even say, \"Hey, it's cool, you're operating this freight elevator, you have the lever,\" my body is already in full meltdown mode. It's like my nervous system doesn't care who's in charge. It just hears that *clunk* and goes, \"Nope, we're in danger.\" I remember one time I was just walking past the freight elevator at work, not even intending to use it, just carrying some training binders to the stairwell, and one of the maintenance guys called it. Just hearing the gears grind and the doors clatter open... bam. Sweaty hands, tight chest, that huge rush of panic. I had to just stand there for a second. \n\nSo yeah, manual control sounds great in theory, but when the panic hits you that fast, before you even cross the threshold, having a lever to pull just doesn't matter at all. Because by the time I'd even get my hands on that lever, I'm already terrified.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced anxiety or fear in situations that don't involve elevators but might still be related to loss of control or unexpected events?\n\nPatient: No, honestly, not at all. Which is... But I'm really not. \n\nLike, take my job, for instance. Being a training and development specialist, especially at our corporate office where things are always kind of chaotic and disorganized... my whole day is basically just managing unexpected events and things totally out of my control. No slides, no training modules, nothing. And I didn't panic even a little bit. I just sort of pivoted, you know? I started doing icebreakers and just whiteboarding the core concepts instead. It was totally out of my control, completely unexpected, a total derailment of my whole schedule, but I was completely fine. My heart rate didn't even go up. \n\nAnd it's the same with other stuff outside of work, too. Like flying on airplanes, for example. You're literally stuck in a tube miles up in the air, totally at the mercy of some pilot you've never met, and that doesn't bother me in the slightest. I just put my headphones on and go to sleep. Or being stuck in crazy bumper-to-bumper traffic on the interstate where you're just boxed in by semi-trucks and you can't move an inch for an hour. A lot of people hate that feeling of being trapped or not being the one able to move, but I just turn up the radio and wait it out. \n\nSo it's really not a control freak thing, you know? I don't need to be in charge of every little thing in my life to feel safe. I'm actually a really go-with-the-flow kind of guy most of the time. It is literally, one hundred percent, just the elevators. If it doesn't involve a metal box hanging by a cable in a dark shaft, I'm totally cool. It’s just that one specific, mechanical scenario that flips that panic switch in my brain because of what happened when we were moving. I work as a training and development specialist—I teach computer skills, run corporate workshops, that sort of thing—and I actually had to turn down this really great workshop opportunity recently. It was going to be held in this massive high-rise downtown, and I just knew I couldn't do the stairs for, like, thirty floors, so I just made up an excuse and didn't go. \n\nI even had to stop visiting one of my favorite clients. He's this older guy I was tutoring, really nice guy, we were making great progress getting him comfortable with his computer and his emails and everything, but I had to stop going to his place because his building doesn’t really have another option besides the elevator. The stairwell is for emergencies only or something, so you can't really use it. So I just had to drop him as a student. I'm just spending so much time and energy trying to avoid them, and it's starting to affect my work and my life, so I figured I probably need to finally talk to someone about it.\n\nDoctor: Is there something specific about elevators that scares you or makes you anxious?\n\nPatient: Well, it's... I’ll be standing there in the lobby, looking at the doors, and my rational brain is sitting there saying, \"Come on, man, thousands of people ride these every single day, the odds of it falling are basically zero.\" But my body and my subconscious are just screaming that it's a death trap. It's this weird split in my head. So even if you put a giant, state-of-the-art emergency phone right in the middle of the wall, or gave me a manual steering wheel for the thing, I’d still be looking at those old doors feeling like I was about to plummet. The logic of a safety feature just doesn't even touch the fear, if that makes sense.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your fear of elevators would be lessened if you were the one operating the elevator, such as in a freight elevator where you have manual control?\n\nPatient: Man, a freight elevator... you know, we actually have one of those at the corporate office I was telling you about. I just feel this absolute, overwhelming rush of panic, and it happens before I’ve even had a split second to think it through. \n\nSo, before my brain can even say, \"Hey, it's cool, you're operating this freight elevator, you have the lever,\" my body is already in full meltdown mode. It's like my nervous system doesn't care who's in charge. I had to just stand there for a second. \n\nSo yeah, manual control sounds great in theory, but when the panic hits you that fast, before you even cross the threshold, having a lever to pull just doesn't matter at all. Because by the time I'd even get my hands on that lever, I'm already terrified.\n\nDoctor: Have you experienced anxiety or fear in situations that don't involve elevators but might still be related to loss of control or unexpected events?\n\nPatient: No, honestly, not at all. I really, truly don't think so. I mean, it’s a fair question, and I get why you'd ask that, because it seems like it would go hand-in-hand, right? But like I was saying earlier with the train and the boat, the 'small space' thing just doesn't register as a threat to me. And even if you add the 'no way out' part... it still doesn't really fit.

No, honestly, I don't think that would help me at all. Not even a little bit. 

I mean, I can totally see the logic behind the question, right? Like, if you're afraid of a machine, just bring along the guy who knows how to fix the machine. It makes sense on paper. The mechanic can't stop gravity, you know? So, yeah, mechanic or no mechanic, expert or no expert, the second I step over that threshold and those heavy metal doors slide shut, that immediate, visceral wave of panic is going to hit me exactly the same way. I'd probably just be standing there, completely frozen and sweating, right next to this poor mechanic who's just trying to ride up to the fourth floor. It’s funny you bring up train cars, actually, because my commute downtown to the corporate office—the one in that older building I was telling you about—I actually take the light rail every single morning. And man, sometimes, especially on Tuesdays and Thursdays when it seems like literally everyone is coming into the office, they pack us in there like absolute sardines. I mean, you are shoulder-to-shoulder with people, you've got someone's backpack shoved into your ribs, the doors are closed, and you're just stuck in this crowded metal tube underground between stations for, you know, five or ten minutes at a time if there's a delay. And... I don't feel a thing. No panic, no sweaty palms, nothing. I just put on a podcast or review my training notes for the day and I'm completely fine. \n\nAnd boats, too! A couple of years ago, right after high school, before I got into the whole training and development field, some buddies and I rented this tiny little aluminum fishing boat out on the lake. It was incredibly cramped. I mean, you could barely turn around without knocking someone's tackle box or cooler into the water, and we were out there for hours, just completely confined to this tiny little footprint of space floating out on the water. And it was totally fine. It was relaxing, actually! \n\nSo, yeah, it's definitely not a claustrophobia thing. It's really not about the size of the room or being confined or trapped in a small area. Like I was saying before with that cramped conference room, I can be in a tiny space, or a packed train, or a little boat, and I'm completely golden. It's just... I don't know, it's just the elevator. The moment you add the cables and the shaft and those heavy mechanical doors, that's the only time my brain completely loses it. Everything else is just totally normal for me.\n\nDoctor: Would you feel anxious or fearful in a situation where you are in a small, enclosed space with mechanical parts, such as a submarine or an MRI machine?\n\nPatient: An MRI machine? Or a submarine? Honestly, no, not at all. I mean, I’ve never been in a submarine, obviously, but I actually had an MRI once back in high school for a minor sports thing, and yeah, it’s a tiny little tube, and it makes all those incredibly loud, clanking, heavy mechanical noises right next to your head, but I just laid there. I think I almost fell asleep, actually. It didn’t bother me one bit. \n\nIt really, truly is just elevators. And the most frustrating part about it—the part that just drives me absolutely crazy when I sit down and try to analyze it—is that I *know* it doesn't make sense. Like, logically, I know an elevator in a standard, modern office block is probably totally safe. I know they have emergency brakes, and counterweights, and regular city inspections, and all those safety regulations, right? I even read up on it once, trying to convince myself to just get over it and look at the facts. \n\nBut it just doesn't matter what the facts are. When I look at those old doors... like the really heavy, outdated ones in my apartment building, or that clunky freight elevator at work, my mind just completely bypasses all that logic. It just immediately treats it like I’m about to get trapped in there for hours, or like the cable is just going to snap and I'm going to get dropped straight down the shaft. It's like a movie playing in my head that I can't turn off. And I'll be standing there, and part of me is literally telling myself, \"Hey, you know this sounds completely over the top, you know this is ridiculous, millions of people ride these every day,\" but the other part of my brain just completely takes over anyway. It's like my logical brain and my survival brain are completely disconnected. So yeah, MRIs, submarines, whatever—totally fine. But those old elevator doors? It's just a completely different story.\n\nDoctor: Would you feel anxious or fearful if you were in an elevator that wasn't moving, such as one that was stuck on a floor or being used for storage?\n\nPatient: Oh, man, yeah. Even if it was completely turned off and just sitting there... I would still absolutely hate it. Because it's not just the motion, you know? It's the whole... the whole presence of the thing. Like, I don't even have to be inside it or moving for the reaction to start. \n\nHonestly, as soon as I even just step toward an elevator, or if I'm walking down the hall and I hear that loud mechanical clunk of the doors sliding open, it's like a switch flips instantly. My chest gets incredibly tight, and my hands get completely sweaty, and I just feel this massive rush of panic flood my system before I've even had a split second to think it through or rationalize it. It's just an immediate, totally visceral reaction. \n\nI actually remember a few months ago, they were doing maintenance on the older elevator in my apartment building. So it was completely shut down, the power was off, and they had the doors propped wide open while the repair guy was getting tools. It was just sitting there on the lobby floor, completely out of service. And I had to walk past it to get to the stairwell, and even though I *knew* it wasn't going anywhere, even though I knew it was essentially just an empty closet at that moment... just looking into that box and walking near it set me off. My chest clamped up, my palms were instantly slick with sweat, and I had that same exact wave of panic just from being near the open doors. \n\nSo, yeah, if one was just being used for storage or it was permanently stuck on a floor? I still wouldn't be able to step foot inside it, let alone hang out in there. The second I get near those doors, the panic is already happening, whether the thing is operational or not. It's like my body just completely takes over and reacts before my logical brain even catches up to the fact that it's turned off.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your fear of elevators is related to the fear of being trapped in a small space with no way out?\n\nPatient: I really, truly don't think so. I mean, it’s a fair question, and I get why you'd ask that, because it seems like it would go hand-in-hand, right? And even if you add the 'no way out' part... it still doesn't really fit. \n\nActually, it’s funny you phrase it exactly like that—'no way out'—because I've thought about that exact concept before. Like, take that light rail commute I mentioned. Sometimes the train stops dead in the dark tunnel between stations because of signal issues ahead. The doors are locked, there's just solid concrete inches away on the outside, and you literally cannot leave. You are one hundred percent trapped with no way out until the driver gets clearance to move again. And... I don't care. It doesn't bother me in the slightest. I just sit there and scroll on my phone or go over my schedule. \n\nOr, oh, here's a perfect example! Last year, my department—the training and development team—we did one of those escape rooms for a team-building exercise. And the whole entire premise of the place is that they lock you in a small, windowless room and you have absolutely no way out for an hour unless you solve the puzzles. I mean, sure, they tell you there's a fire exit, but you're essentially trapped in there. And I had an absolute blast! I was the one organizing all the clues on the table, totally in the zone, having a great time. No sweaty palms, no tight chest, absolutely no panic. \n\nSo, yeah, it's really not the 'trapped' part. It's not about being locked in or not having an exit. If it was just about being stuck somewhere I couldn't leave, I'd be freaking out on airplanes, or in that escape room, or on the train underground. But I'm completely fine in all those situations. It's just... it's the elevator itself. It's the hanging by a cable, the empty shaft underneath, the specific mechanical reality of what an elevator is. The 'no way out' thing just doesn't trigger my brain at all unless the room I can't get out of happens to be dangling in an elevator shaft.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your fear of elevators is related to the loss of control you experience when you're inside one?\n\nPatient: Loss of control? Hmm. You know, I’ve actually spent a lot of time turning that exact idea over in my head, because my girlfriend actually suggested the exact same thing a couple of months ago. She was like, \"Maybe you just hate not being the one driving,\" or, you know, not being the one in charge of the situation. But... no, I really don't think that’s it either. \n\nBecause if you really sit down and think about it, we give up control all the time, right? Like, I fly a couple of times a year for work—mostly going to conferences for the training and development networking stuff—and when you’re sitting in seat 22B on a commercial flight, you have absolutely zero control over what happens. You are completely, one hundred percent at the mercy of the pilots behind a locked door, the air traffic controllers, the weather, the mechanics who checked the engine that morning... and I’m totally fine! I just put my headphones in, watch a movie, maybe ask the flight attendant for a ginger ale, and I don’t even think twice about the fact that I can’t steer the plane or hit the brakes. \n\nOr even something as simple as taking an Uber, you know? You’re getting into a complete stranger's car, they’re the one driving, they're the one navigating traffic, and you’re just sitting in the back seat hoping they know what they’re doing and that their brakes work. And I do that all the time without a second thought. I don't get sweaty palms, my chest doesn't tighten up, I don't panic at all. Or rollercoasters! I love rollercoasters. You get strapped into this little cart, some teenager pushes a button, and you just get whipped around a track with literally no way to stop it or control where you're going. And I think that's incredibly fun. \n\nSo, yeah, it’s really not the control thing. I don’t need to be the one pushing the buttons or steering the ship, so to speak, to feel safe. If it was just a control issue, I feel like I'd be a nervous wreck in Ubers or on planes, but I'm not. It all just comes right back to the elevator itself. The cable, the empty shaft underneath, the heavy doors... that specific mechanical setup. It’s not about who’s driving it or whether I'm in charge, it’s just... the machine itself, you know? It's just that one specific thing.\n\nDoctor: Would your fear decrease if you were in an elevator that was moving, but you were accompanied by an elevator mechanic or someone who could fix it if something went wrong?\n\nPatient: No, honestly, I don't think that would help me at all. Not even a little bit. \n\nI mean, I can totally see the logic behind the question, right? Like, if you're afraid of a machine, just bring along the guy who knows how to fix the machine. It makes sense on paper. But... it really wouldn't make a dent in the panic for me, because it's not just about the fear of it breaking down. It's the fact that I am *in* it at all. \n\nEven if you found the absolute best, most highly trained, top-tier elevator mechanic in the entire world, and he was standing right next to me in that little box, holding his toolbox and a clipboard, swearing up and down that everything is perfectly safe... my chest would still be incredibly tight. My palms would still be completely slick with sweat. Because, you know, even if he's standing right there, we are still just two guys suspended by a cable in a giant, empty concrete tube. His presence doesn't change the physical reality of what an elevator is, if that makes sense? He can't magically make the empty shaft underneath us disappear. \n\nAnd honestly, if you really think about it, having a mechanic in there with me might actually make my brain spiral even more. Because if I'm in an elevator and I see a guy in a maintenance uniform with a bunch of wrenches and diagnostic tools, I'm immediately going to be thinking, 'Wait, why is he in here? Is he expecting something to snap? Did he hear a weird grinding noise that I didn't hear? Is the cable fraying?' Like, I know you meant it as a hypothetical where he's just there to be a safety net and make me feel better, but my brain would instantly jump to the conclusion that the elevator is actively failing right at that exact second and that's why he's there. \n\nBut even putting all of that aside, even if I knew for a one hundred percent absolute fact that he was just riding along to keep me company... it just wouldn't matter. The mechanic can't stop gravity, you know? Like I was saying before with that cramped conference room, I can be in a tiny space, or a packed train, or a little boat, and I'm completely golden. It's just... I don't know, it's just the elevator. The moment you add the cables and the shaft and those heavy mechanical doors, that's the only time my brain completely loses it. Everything else is just totally normal for me.\n\nDoctor: Would you feel anxious or fearful in a situation where you are in a small, enclosed space with mechanical parts, such as a submarine or an MRI machine?\n\nPatient: An MRI machine? Or a submarine? Honestly, no, not at all. I mean, I’ve never been in a submarine, obviously, but I actually had an MRI once back in high school for a minor sports thing, and yeah, it’s a tiny little tube, and it makes all those incredibly loud, clanking, heavy mechanical noises right next to your head, but I just laid there. I think I almost fell asleep, actually. It didn’t bother me one bit. \n\nIt really, truly is just elevators. And the most frustrating part about it—the part that just drives me absolutely crazy when I sit down and try to analyze it—is that I *know* it doesn't make sense. Like, logically, I know an elevator in a standard, modern office block is probably totally safe. I know they have emergency brakes, and counterweights, and regular city inspections, and all those safety regulations, right? I even read up on it once, trying to convince myself to just get over it and look at the facts. \n\nBut it just doesn't matter what the facts are. When I look at those old doors... like the really heavy, outdated ones in my apartment building, or that clunky freight elevator at work, my mind just completely bypasses all that logic. It just immediately treats it like I’m about to get trapped in there for hours, or like the cable is just going to snap and I'm going to get dropped straight down the shaft. It's like a movie playing in my head that I can't turn off. And I'll be standing there, and part of me is literally telling myself, \"Hey, you know this sounds completely over the top, you know this is ridiculous, millions of people ride these every day,\" but the other part of my brain just completely takes over anyway. It's like my logical brain and my survival brain are completely disconnected. So yeah, MRIs, submarines, whatever—totally fine. But those old elevator doors? It's just a completely different story.\n\nDoctor: Would you feel anxious or fearful if you were in an elevator that wasn't moving, such as one that was stuck on a floor or being used for storage?\n\nPatient: Oh, man, yeah. Even if it was completely turned off and just sitting there... I would still absolutely hate it. Because it's not just the motion, you know? It's the whole... the whole presence of the thing. Like, I don't even have to be inside it or moving for the reaction to start. \n\nHonestly, as soon as I even just step toward an elevator, or if I'm walking down the hall and I hear that loud mechanical clunk of the doors sliding open, it's like a switch flips instantly. My chest gets incredibly tight, and my hands get completely sweaty, and I just feel this massive rush of panic flood my system before I've even had a split second to think it through or rationalize it. It's just an immediate, totally visceral reaction. \n\nI actually remember a few months ago, they were doing maintenance on the older elevator in my apartment building. So it was completely shut down, the power was off, and they had the doors propped wide open while the repair guy was getting tools. It was just sitting there on the lobby floor, completely out of service. And I had to walk past it to get to the stairwell, and even though I *knew* it wasn't going anywhere, even though I knew it was essentially just an empty closet at that moment... just looking into that box and walking near it set me off. My chest clamped up, my palms were instantly slick with sweat, and I had that same exact wave of panic just from being near the open doors. \n\nSo, yeah, if one was just being used for storage or it was permanently stuck on a floor? I still wouldn't be able to step foot inside it, let alone hang out in there. The second I get near those doors, the panic is already happening, whether the thing is operational or not. It's like my body just completely takes over and reacts before my logical brain even catches up to the fact that it's turned off.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your fear of elevators is related to the fear of being trapped in a small space with no way out?\n\nPatient: I really, truly don't think so. I mean, it’s a fair question, and I get why you'd ask that, because it seems like it would go hand-in-hand, right? But like I was saying earlier with the train and the boat, the 'small space' thing just doesn't register as a threat to me. And even if you add the 'no way out' part... it still doesn't really fit. \n\nActually, it’s funny you phrase it exactly like that—'no way out'—because I've thought about that exact concept before. Like, take that light rail commute I mentioned. Sometimes the train stops dead in the dark tunnel between stations because of signal issues ahead. The doors are locked, there's just solid concrete inches away on the outside, and you literally cannot leave. You are one hundred percent trapped with no way out until the driver gets clearance to move again. And... I don't care. It doesn't bother me in the slightest. I just sit there and scroll on my phone or go over my schedule. \n\nOr, oh, here's a perfect example! Last year, my department—the training and development team—we did one of those escape rooms for a team-building exercise. And the whole entire premise of the place is that they lock you in a small, windowless room and you have absolutely no way out for an hour unless you solve the puzzles. I mean, sure, they tell you there's a fire exit, but you're essentially trapped in there. And I had an absolute blast! I was the one organizing all the clues on the table, totally in the zone, having a great time. No sweaty palms, no tight chest, absolutely no panic. \n\nSo, yeah, it's really not the 'trapped' part. It's not about being locked in or not having an exit. If it was just about being stuck somewhere I couldn't leave, I'd be freaking out on airplanes, or in that escape room, or on the train underground. But I'm completely fine in all those situations. It's just... it's the elevator itself. It's the hanging by a cable, the empty shaft underneath, the specific mechanical reality of what an elevator is. The 'no way out' thing just doesn't trigger my brain at all unless the room I can't get out of happens to be dangling in an elevator shaft.\n\nDoctor: Do you think your fear of elevators is related to the loss of control you experience when you're inside one?\n\nPatient: Loss of control? Hmm. You know, I’ve actually spent a lot of time turning that exact idea over in my head, because my girlfriend actually suggested the exact same thing a couple of months ago. She was like, \"Maybe you just hate not being the one driving,\" or, you know, not being the one in charge of the situation. But... no, I really don't think that’s it either. \n\nBecause if you really sit down and think about it, we give up control all the time, right? Like, I fly a couple of times a year for work—mostly going to conferences for the training and development networking stuff—and when you’re sitting in seat 22B on a commercial flight, you have absolutely zero control over what happens. You are completely, one hundred percent at the mercy of the pilots behind a locked door, the air traffic controllers, the weather, the mechanics who checked the engine that morning... and I’m totally fine! I just put my headphones in, watch a movie, maybe ask the flight attendant for a ginger ale, and I don’t even think twice about the fact that I can’t steer the plane or hit the brakes. \n\nOr even something as simple as taking an Uber, you know? You’re getting into a complete stranger's car, they’re the one driving, they're the one navigating traffic, and you’re just sitting in the back seat hoping they know what they’re doing and that their brakes work. And I do that all the time without a second thought. I don't get sweaty palms, my chest doesn't tighten up, I don't panic at all. Or rollercoasters! I love rollercoasters. You get strapped into this little cart, some teenager pushes a button, and you just get whipped around a track with literally no way to stop it or control where you're going. And I think that's incredibly fun. \n\nSo, yeah, it’s really not the control thing. I don’t need to be the one pushing the buttons or steering the ship, so to speak, to feel safe. If it was just a control issue, I feel like I'd be a nervous wreck in Ubers or on planes, but I'm not. It all just comes right back to the elevator itself. The cable, the empty shaft underneath, the heavy doors... that specific mechanical setup. It’s not about who’s driving it or whether I'm in charge, it’s just... the machine itself, you know? It's just that one specific thing.\n\nDoctor: Would your fear decrease if you were in an elevator that was moving, but you were accompanied by an elevator mechanic or someone who could fix it if something went wrong?\n\nPatient: No, honestly, I don't think that would help me at all. Not even a little bit. \n\nI mean, I can totally see the logic behind the question, right? Like, if you're afraid of a machine, just bring along the guy who knows how to fix the machine. It makes sense on paper. But... it really wouldn't make a dent in the panic for me, because it's not just about the fear of it breaking down. It's the fact that I am *in* it at all. \n\nEven if you found the absolute best, most highly trained, top-tier elevator mechanic in the entire world, and he was standing right next to me in that little box, holding his toolbox and a clipboard, swearing up and down that everything is perfectly safe... my chest would still be incredibly tight. My palms would still be completely slick with sweat. Because, you know, even if he's standing right there, we are still just two guys suspended by a cable in a giant, empty concrete tube. His presence doesn't change the physical reality of what an elevator is, if that makes sense? He can't magically make the empty shaft underneath us disappear. \n\nAnd honestly, if you really think about it, having a mechanic in there with me might actually make my brain spiral even more. Because if I'm in an elevator and I see a guy in a maintenance uniform with a bunch of wrenches and diagnostic tools, I'm immediately going to be thinking, 'Wait, why is he in here? Is he expecting something to snap? Did he hear a weird grinding noise that I didn't hear? Is the cable fraying?' Like, I know you meant it as a hypothetical where he's just there to be a safety net and make me feel better, but my brain would instantly jump to the conclusion that the elevator is actively failing right at that exact second and that's why he's there. \n\nBut even putting all of that aside, even if I knew for a one hundred percent absolute fact that he was just riding along to keep me company... it just wouldn't matter. The mechanic can't stop gravity, you know? I'd probably just be standing there, completely frozen and sweating, right next to this poor mechanic who's just trying to ride up to the fourth floor. It’s just that one specific, mechanical scenario that flips that panic switch in my brain because of what happened when we were moving. Everything else... yeah, I just handle it like a normal person.\n\nDoctor: Do you think you would feel anxious or fearful if you were in a situation where you were confined to a small space, but it wasn't an elevator, such as a small boat or a train car?\n\nPatient: No, honestly, not at all. The height is just the consequence of the fall, not the thing that actually scares me. If that makes any sense.\n\nDoctor: Do you worry about what other people might think of you if you were to have a panic attack or exhibit anxious behavior while in an elevator?\n\nPatient: Honestly, no.
