She was like, \"Maybe you just hate not being the one driving,\" or, you know, not being the one in charge of the situation. But... no, I really don't think that’s it either. \n\nBecause if you really sit down and think about it, we give up control all the time, right? Like, I fly a couple of times a year for work—mostly going to conferences for the training and development networking stuff—and when you’re sitting in seat 22B on a commercial flight, you have absolutely zero control over what happens. You are completely, one hundred percent at the mercy of the pilots behind a locked door, the air traffic controllers, the weather, the mechanics who checked the engine that morning... and I’m totally fine! I just put my headphones in, watch a movie, maybe ask the flight attendant for a ginger ale, and I don’t even think twice about the fact that I can’t steer the plane or hit the brakes. \n\nOr even something as simple as taking an Uber, you know? You’re getting into a complete stranger's car, they’re the one driving, they're the one navigating traffic, and you’re just sitting in the back seat hoping they know what they’re doing and that their brakes work. And I do that all the time without a second thought. I don't get sweaty palms, my chest doesn't tighten up, I don't panic at all. Or rollercoasters! I love rollercoasters. You get strapped into this little cart, some teenager pushes a button, and you just get whipped around a track with literally no way to stop it or control where you're going. And I think that's incredibly fun. \n\nSo, yeah, it’s really not the control thing. I don’t need to be the one pushing the buttons or steering the ship, so to speak, to feel safe. If it was just a control issue, I feel like I'd be a nervous wreck in Ubers or on planes, but I'm not. It all just comes right back to the elevator itself. The cable, the empty shaft underneath, the heavy doors... that specific mechanical setup. It’s not about who’s driving it or whether I'm in charge, it’s just... the machine itself, you know? It's just that one specific thing.\n\nDoctor: Would your fear decrease if you were in an elevator that was moving, but you were accompanied by an elevator mechanic or someone who could fix it if something went wrong?\n\nPatient: No, honestly, I don't think that would help me at all. Not even a little bit. \n\nI mean, I can totally see the logic behind the question, right? Like, if you're afraid of a machine, just bring along the guy who knows how to fix the machine. It makes sense on paper. But... it really wouldn't make a dent in the panic for me, because it's not just about the fear of it breaking down. It's the fact that I am *in* it at all. \n\nEven if you found the absolute best, most highly trained, top-tier elevator mechanic in the entire world, and he was standing right next to me in that little box, holding his toolbox and a clipboard, swearing up and down that everything is perfectly safe... my chest would still be incredibly tight. My palms would still be completely slick with sweat. Because, you know, even if he's standing right there, we are still just two guys suspended by a cable in a giant, empty concrete tube. His presence doesn't change the physical reality of what an elevator is, if that makes sense? He can't magically make the empty shaft underneath us disappear. \n\nAnd honestly, if you really think about it, having a mechanic in there with me might actually make my brain spiral even more. Because if I'm in an elevator and I see a guy in a maintenance uniform with a bunch of wrenches and diagnostic tools, I'm immediately going to be thinking, 'Wait, why is he in here? Is he expecting something to snap? Did he hear a weird grinding noise that I didn't hear? Is the cable fraying?' Like, I know you meant it as a hypothetical where he's just there to be a safety net and make me feel better, but my brain would instantly jump to the conclusion that the elevator is actively failing right at that exact second and that's why he's there. \n\nBut even putting all of that aside, even if I knew for a one hundred percent absolute fact that he was just riding along to keep me company... it just wouldn't matter. The mechanic can't stop gravity, you know? So, yeah, mechanic or no mechanic, expert or no expert, the second I step over that threshold and those heavy metal doors slide shut, that immediate, visceral wave of panic is going to hit me exactly the same way. I'd probably just be standing there, completely frozen and sweating, right next to this poor mechanic who's just trying to ride up to the fourth floor. So, no, it really wouldn't decrease the fear for me at all.\n\nDoctor: Would you feel anxious or fearful if you were in an elevator that was moving horizontally, like a people mover or a funicular?\n\nPatient: A people mover? Like the ones they have at the airport? Oh, no, I’m completely fine on those. Actually, I was just on one of those a few months ago when I was flying out to Chicago for a training seminar, and you just stand there with your luggage and it glides you down the terminal. It’s totally fine, because you’re just sliding along the solid ground. And a funicular... I mean, that's on a track on a hill, right? I think I'd be okay with that too, because, again, there's solid ground right underneath the track. It's not dangling in mid-air. \n\nSo, yeah, horizontal movement doesn't bother me at all. It really just comes back to that vertical drop and the specific setup of an actual elevator. And the funny thing is, logically, I know an elevator in a big, modern office block is probably completely safe. I know they have emergency brakes and sensors and regular inspections and all that. But... man, when I look at those old doors in my apartment building, or even the older elevators we have over at my work—they have these heavy, clunky metal doors that kind of rattle and groan when they slide shut—my mind just instantly treats it like I’m about to get trapped in there, or the cable is going to snap and I'm going to get dropped straight down the shaft. \n\nI mean, part of me knows that sounds completely over the top, you know? I'm a rational guy. I know it's highly unlikely. But the second I stand in front of those old doors and hear that mechanical clank, all that logic just completely flies right out the window. It's like my brain just overrides the rational part that says 'hey, millions of people ride these safely every single day.' I just stand there staring at the gap between the floor and the elevator car, imagining the whole thing just giving way. So, yeah, a people mover is a breeze, it's just... those vertical ones, especially the older ones, that just completely mess with my head, even when I know I'm being ridiculous about it.\n\nDoctor: Would your fear of elevators decrease if you were in a vertically moving elevator that was completely transparent, allowing you to see the surrounding shaft and mechanics at all times?\n\nPatient: Oh, wow. A completely transparent one? Um... I'm honestly not sure. I don't think I've ever actually been in a fully transparent elevator inside a working shaft like that, so I can't say for one hundred percent certain how I'd react. But... man, just picturing it in my head right now? I really, really don't think that would decrease my fear at all. \n\nBecause, like I was saying earlier, the empty space underneath the car is the main thing my brain fixates on. So if the floor is clear, and the walls are clear, and I can literally look down between my shoes and see a dark, fifty-foot drop to the bottom of the concrete pit? Yeah, no, that sounds absolutely terrifying. I mean, I guess I see what you're getting at—like, if I can see the cables and the brakes, maybe my brain would see that they're thick and strong and working properly, right? But for me, seeing all those gears and greasy tracks and huge counterweights rushing past... it would just be way too much visual information. It would just constantly remind me of exactly how high up I am and how I'm just dangling there in the middle of nowhere. \n\nAt least in a regular, closed-off elevator—as much as I hate those old clunky doors—you can kind of try to trick your brain for a second. You can stare at the floor numbers lighting up, or read the little inspection certificate framed on the wall, or just look at the carpet and pretend you're just standing in a really small closet for a minute. But if the whole thing is glass, and you're just staring at raw concrete walls sliding past you in this giant, hollow tube... there's no pretending. You can't ignore the physical reality of where you are. \n\nI remember being at this fancy hotel atrium once, years ago, where they had those glass elevators that look out over the lobby, and even just watching the ground floor get further and further away made my stomach do flip-flops. And that was just looking at a nice lobby, not a dark mechanical shaft! So, yeah, I can't say for sure since I haven't actually been in a fully transparent shaft elevator, but I'm pretty confident it would just force me to look at the exact things I'm most afraid of. I'd probably just end up squeezing my eyes shut and sitting on the floor until the doors opened.\n\nDoctor: Would your fear decrease if you were in an elevator that moved vertically, but had a safety harness or a secondary support system to prevent falling?\n\nPatient: A safety harness? Like... like strapped into the elevator itself? Honestly, I have absolutely no idea. I don't think I could even give you a straight answer on that because I've never even heard of a setup like that in a normal building. \n\nI mean, I do a lot of onboarding and development training at my job, and part of that is going over basic workplace safety, emergency exits, that kind of thing. But I have never in my life seen an elevator where you have to clip in. How would that even work, logistically? Would there just be a bunch of carabiners hanging from the ceiling? Like you're at an indoor rock climbing gym or something? Because if I'm just standing there in my work clothes, holding my coffee, and I have to strap into a five-point harness just to go up to the fourth floor... I feel like that alone would make me hyper-aware that something terrible could happen. \n\nBut as for whether it would actually decrease the fear... I really don't know. Because my brain immediately starts picking apart the mechanics of it. Like, what exactly is this harness attached to? Is it attached to the ceiling of the elevator car? Because if the cable snaps and the whole car falls, the ceiling goes right down with it, right? So then I'm just securely strapped into a falling metal box, which honestly almost sounds worse because I wouldn't even be able to brace myself. \n\nOr, wait, do you mean it's attached to a completely separate, secondary cable system? Like an independent line that goes all the way up to the roof? I guess if it's a completely separate line, that makes a little more sense on paper. But even then... say the floor gives out or the car drops, and the harness catches me. Now I'm just dangling in mid-air in a pitch-black elevator shaft, completely alone, just swinging there by a strap while I wait for the fire department to show up. Which, sure, is definitely better than falling fifty feet to the concrete pit, I will absolutely give you that. But just picturing myself hanging there in the dark, looking down into that empty space... my heart is actually racing a little bit just talking about it right now. \n\nSo, yeah, I honestly couldn't tell you if it would help. I really don't know. It’s just such a bizarre scenario to try and picture. I think the whole process of putting on a harness would just remind me of exactly what I’m terrified of, but maybe the physical sensation of being held up would counteract it? I just don't have a good answer for you on that one, because my mind just keeps spinning out all these weird hypothetical scenarios of me dangling in the shaft.\n\nDoctor: Did the traumatic experience of being stuck in an elevator contribute to the development of your fear of elevators?\n\nPatient: Oh, absolutely. Yeah, one hundred percent. That is exactly where all of this started. It’s actually been going on for about seven months now, basically ever since that specific incident. \n\nI had just moved into this new place—well, it’s an older building, like I was telling you about earlier with those heavy, clunky metal doors, but it was a new apartment for me. It’s up on the fifth floor, which I was actually really excited about at first because it gets a lot of natural light and has a nice view, you know? But man, shortly after I moved in, I had that massive elevator scare, and everything just completely shifted for me after that. \n\nBefore that day, I swear, I never even thought twice about getting into an elevator. I’d just walk in, press the button, check my work emails on my phone, and totally tune out until the doors opened. But ever since that scare... I mean, for the last seven months, my brain just won't let it go. It’s like a switch flipped. I’ve literally been trudging up five flights of stairs every single day with my groceries, my work bag, my laundry, just to avoid getting back into that thing. And it didn't just stay at the apartment, either; it bled over into the elevators at my job, too, which makes doing my training sessions a huge hassle if I have to bounce between floors. \n\nSo, yeah, to answer your question, it all traces directly back to that one terrifying experience seven months ago, right after I got that fifth-floor place. If I had just rented a ground-floor unit, maybe I wouldn't even be sitting here talking to you about this right now, you know? But yeah... seven months of just completely overthinking it and taking the stairs."
